title: The Glow That Was Not Safe

pages.text: Some watches have hands and numbers that shine pale green in the dark, so you can read the time at night without a lamp. Today the paint that glows is harmless. It simply soaks up light and gives it out again slowly. A hundred years ago, the glow came from something very different: a newly discovered metal called radium, which shone by itself day and night for years on end. People thought it was a wonder. The story of the women who painted it onto watch faces changed the way the world protects its workers.

pages.text: In 1896, the French scientist Henri Becquerel found that a rock containing uranium darkened a photographic plate even when wrapped in black paper. Something invisible was coming out of it. Marie Curie named this effect radioactivity. In 1898, she and her husband Pierre discovered radium, which was far more active than uranium. We now know that some atoms have an unstable nucleus. Sooner or later it breaks down and shoots out radiation. This radiation carries enough energy to damage living cells. Nothing you do to the material, such as heating, cooling, or crushing it, can switch it off.

pages.text: Doctors soon found that radium could shrink cancer tumours. From this, many people leapt to a false idea: that radium must be healthy for everybody. Companies sold radium water, radium toothpaste, and radium face creams that promised a youthful glow. Nobody had tested them. Meanwhile, the scientists who handled radium every day were becoming ill. Marie Curie herself died in 1934 of a blood disease caused by years of exposure. Her notebooks are still radioactive today and are kept in lead-lined boxes. The danger was real, but it took years to show.

pages.text: From 1917, factories in the United States hired thousands of young women to paint watch and clock dials with glowing radium paint. The pay was good and the work was clean. To paint fine numbers, the women were told to bring the brush to a point between their lips, again and again, hundreds of times a day. Each time, they swallowed a little radium. They were told it was harmless. The body treats radium like calcium and stores it in the bones. There it stays, giving out radiation from the inside for the rest of a person’s life.

pages.text: Within a few years, the women’s teeth fell out and their jaws and bones began to crumble. Many developed cancers, and some died. The factory owners denied that radium was to blame. Five sick women took one company to court and won a settlement in 1928. Another case went on until 1939. Their courage changed the law. Employers became responsible for illnesses caused by work, and safety limits for radiation were set. Ask who pays the price today when workers are not told the truth about dust, chemicals, or the mercury used in illegal gold mining.

pages.text: Radiation is not only man-made. A little reaches us all the time from rocks, soil, food, and space. This is called background radiation, and our bodies cope with it. Used with care, stronger radiation does great good. Hospitals use it to find and treat disease. At Kwabenya, near Accra, a radiation facility sterilises medical supplies and helps to preserve food. Three rules keep workers safe: spend as little time near the source as possible, keep your distance, and put shielding such as lead or thick concrete in between. Radiation is safe when science, honesty, and the law work together.

activities.question: What is radioactivity?
options: The giving out of radiation by unstable nuclei
The glow of paint that has soaked up light
Heat produced by rubbing two metals together

activities.question: What mistake did people make about radium in the early 1900s?
options: They believed it was too rare to use
They thought it could not glow
They assumed that because it treated cancer it must be healthy for everyone

activities.question: Why did swallowed radium do so much harm?
options: It dissolved the stomach at once
The body stored it in the bones, where it gave out radiation for life
It stopped the women from breathing

activities.question: Apply it: A worker must check a radioactive source in a factory. Which plan follows the three safety rules?
options: Work quickly, use long-handled tools, and stand behind a lead screen
Hold the source close to see it clearly and take plenty of time
Carry the source in a shirt pocket

activities.prompt: Put these events in order, from earliest to latest.
items: Becquerel notices invisible rays from uranium
Marie and Pierre Curie discover radium
Factories hire women to paint dials with radium paint
Five sick workers win a settlement in court
Marie Curie dies of an illness caused by radiation

activities.definition: Energy sent out as rays or fast particles, for example from unstable nuclei.
distractors: A glow that comes from fresh paint
A metal used to make watch cases

glossary.definition: A radioactive metal that glows faintly in the dark.
The giving out of radiation by unstable nuclei.
The tiny, heavy centre of an atom.
Energy sent out as rays or fast particles.
Background radiation: the low level of radiation that is always around us from natural sources.
Material such as lead or concrete placed between a person and a source of radiation.
